title: Hypersensitivity
covers: Immune tolerance and the four Gell and Coombs types of hypersensitivity: mechanisms, timing, clinical examples and how type I is diagnosed.

items.p: Immune tolerance is an active state of unresponsiveness to specific antigens. Self-tolerance means no response to the body's own antigens; when it fails, the result is autoimmunity.
Hypersensitivity is an excessive reaction to an antigen that is normally harmless. It can be mild (urticaria) or life-threatening (anaphylaxis), local or systemic.

summary.h: The four types at a glance

table: Allergic rhinitis, asthma, food allergy, anaphylaxis
Transfusion reaction, Rh disease, Goodpasture, Graves, myasthenia gravis
Contact dermatitis, tuberculin test, graft rejection

items.p: Types I, II and III need antibody. Type IV is T cells and cytokines.
First exposure sensitizes. Th2 cells (driven by IL-4) make B cells switch to IgE, and IgE coats mast cells and basophils through the high-affinity receptor FcεRI.
On re-exposure the allergen cross-links IgE and the cells degranulate within minutes.

ul: Preformed: histamine, tryptase, chymase
Newly made: prostaglandins, leukotrienes (strong bronchoconstrictors), Th2 cytokines
IL-5: eosinophils. IL-13: mucus and smooth-muscle contraction.
Early phase: starts in 5–30 minutes, lasts about an hour
Late phase: starts in 2–7 hours, lasts days; eosinophils and neutrophils are recruited

items.p: Atopy is the inherited tendency to make IgE against common allergens. IgE has the lowest plasma level, the shortest half-life (about 2 days) and does not cross the placenta.

ul: Skin tests: prick, scratch or intradermal. Read the wheal and redness at 15–20 minutes.
Controls: histamine (positive) and saline (negative)
Antihistamines give false negatives
Allergen-specific IgE in blood: preferred when anaphylaxis is a real risk
Total IgE: often high, but a normal value does not exclude allergy
Tryptase: marker of mast-cell activation
Provocation test and elimination diet when the picture is unclear

items.p: Antibody binds an antigen fixed on a cell or tissue. Three possible results:

ul: The cell is destroyed quietly (opsonization and phagocytosis, or ADCC)
Complement is activated and inflammation follows
The cell survives but works abnormally

items.p: Examples of abnormal function: in Graves disease the antibody stimulates the TSH receptor; in myasthenia gravis it blocks the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor.
Goodpasture syndrome: antibody against basement membrane in lung and kidney, with lung bleeding and glomerulonephritis.
Rh disease: a sensitized Rh-negative mother makes antibody against the D antigen on fetal red cells.
Complexes of antibody and soluble antigen settle in vessel walls, joints, glomeruli and alveoli. Complement is activated and inflammation damages the tissue.

ul: Arthus reaction: local. Antigen injected into the skin of someone who already has antibody. Local vasculitis 4–12 hours later (seen rarely after tetanus or diphtheria toxoid).
Serum sickness: systemic. Large dose of foreign protein such as antivenom. Fever, rash and joint pain 7–10 days later. Stop the agent.
Lupus: complexes with anti-nuclear antibodies

items.p: Two phases: sensitization (7–10 days, memory T cells form), then damage 1–2 days after the next contact.

ul: CD4 T cells: delayed-type hypersensitivity. IL-12 gives Th1 cells, IFN-γ calls in macrophages, and their enzymes and oxygen radicals injure tissue. IL-6 gives Th17 cells, and IL-17 calls in neutrophils.
CD8 T cells: direct killing. Graft rejection, Hashimoto disease.

items.p: Remember the 5 Ts: T cells, Transplant rejection, TB skin test, Touching (contact dermatitis), Terminal (delayed).
The patch test diagnoses contact dermatitis. Poison ivy acts through urushiol, a chemical that alters self proteins.

items.note: The slide names type IV "cytotoxic T lymphocyte mediated". The detailed slides and standard texts split it into CD4-mediated (delayed-type) and CD8-mediated (cytotoxic) reactions.

cards.a: An active state of unresponsiveness to specific antigens; loss of self-tolerance gives autoimmunity.

cards.q: Gell and Coombs: the four types in one line each
cards.a: I: IgE, immediate. II: antibody against cell-bound antigen. III: immune complexes. IV: T cells, delayed.
Types I, II and III (type IV is T-cell mediated)

cards.q: Which cytokine drives Th2 differentiation and IgE switching?
cards.a: IL-4

cards.q: The receptor that holds IgE on mast cells
cards.a: FcεRI (high-affinity IgE receptor)

cards.q: What triggers mast-cell degranulation in type I?
cards.a: The allergen cross-links IgE already bound to the cell.
Histamine and neutral proteases (tryptase, chymase)
IL-5: eosinophil growth, activation and survival. IL-13: mucus and smooth-muscle contraction.

cards.q: Early versus late phase of type I
cards.a: Early: 5–30 minutes, about an hour. Late: 2–7 hours, lasts days, eosinophils and neutrophils.
Genetic predisposition to make IgE against common allergens (asthma, rhinoconjunctivitis, atopic dermatitis)
Lowest plasma level, shortest half-life (about 2 days), no placental transfer

cards.q: When is an allergy skin test read, and with which controls?
cards.a: 15–20 minutes; histamine positive control, saline negative control

cards.q: Common cause of a false-negative skin test
cards.a: Antihistamines taken beforehand

cards.q: Which test when anaphylaxis risk is high?
cards.a: Allergen-specific IgE in blood, instead of skin testing
Mast-cell activation; a high level signals risk of severe reactions

cards.q: Three outcomes of antibody binding to a cell (type II)
cards.a: Destruction without inflammation, complement activation with inflammation, or dysfunction without destruction
Antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor: hyperthyroidism
Antibodies block postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors: weakness and fatigue
Antibodies against basement membrane of lung and kidney: lung bleeding and glomerulonephritis

cards.q: How do immune complexes injure tissue (type III)?
cards.a: They deposit in vessels, joints, glomeruli and alveoli and activate complement.
Local type III: antigen injected into skin of a sensitized person; vasculitis in 4–12 hours
Systemic type III after foreign protein (antivenom): fever, rash, joint pain at 7–10 days; stop the agent

cards.q: Two forms of type IV hypersensitivity
cards.a: CD4: delayed-type hypersensitivity (macrophages). CD8: direct cytotoxicity.
IL-12 → Th1 → IFN-γ → macrophages → TNF-α, IL-1β → tissue damage
T cells, Transplant rejection, TB skin test, Touching (contact dermatitis), Terminal (delayed)
Patch test

questions.stem: How does the lecture define immune tolerance?

options.A: A passive absence of lymphocytes specific for an antigen not yet encountered
options.B: An excessive reaction to naturally harmless antigens
options.C: A waning of the response after the antigen is cleared
options.D: A genetic tendency to produce IgE to common allergens
options.E: An active state of unresponsiveness to specific antigens

questions.explanation: Immune tolerance is an active state of unresponsiveness to specific antigens that prevents destructive over-reactivity. Self-tolerance means no response to antigens produced by the body itself; its failure is autoimmunity. A: Tolerance is described as an active state. B: That is hypersensitivity. C: That is self-limitation. D: That is atopy.

questions.stem: Which statement about hypersensitivity is correct?

options.A: An excessive reaction to naturally harmless antigens
options.B: A deficient reaction to pathogenic antigens that range from viruses to helminths
options.C: An appropriate reaction to self antigens that is limited to the skin
options.D: An excessive reaction that is life-threatening in each case, as in urticaria
options.E: A reaction that requires injection of the allergen to occur

questions.explanation: Hypersensitivity is an inappropriate excessive reaction to naturally "harmless" antigens, ranging from mild (cutaneous urticaria) to life-threatening (anaphylaxis); symptoms can be local or systemic. B: Hypersensitivity is an excessive, inappropriate reaction. C: It is inappropriate and can be systemic. D: Severity ranges from mild (urticaria) to life-threatening (anaphylaxis). E: Exposure can also be by ingestion, inhalation or contact.

questions.stem: Each of the following is listed as a route of exposure to allergens EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Exposure to allergens can occur through ingestion, inhalation, injection and physical contact. Allergens can be environmental (dust, pollens, food products) or drug components. A: Listed. B: Listed. C: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: On what basis does the Gell and Coombs classification group hypersensitivity reactions into four types?

options.A: The organ affected and the severity of the reaction
options.B: The route of exposure and the dose of the allergen
options.C: The mechanism involved and the time taken for the reaction
options.D: The antibody class involved and the patient's age at onset
options.E: The chemical nature of the antigen and its molecular weight

questions.explanation: Based on the Gell and Coombs classification (early 1960s), reactions are grouped into 4 types according to the mechanism involved and the time taken for the reaction. A: Not the basis given. B: Not the basis given. D: Not the basis given. E: Not the basis given.

questions.stem: A boy develops glomerulonephritis two weeks after a streptococcal throat infection. What mechanism causes the kidney damage?
questions.explanation: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is a type III (immune complex) reaction. A: Type I. C: Goodpasture (type II). D: Type IV. E: Type IV.

questions.stem: What mediates type IV hypersensitivity?
questions.explanation: Types I, II and III are antibody-mediated; type IV is mediated by T cells and cytokines. A: Type I. B: Type II. C: Type III. E: Not a type.

questions.stem: Which antigen form is targeted in type II hypersensitivity?
questions.explanation: Type I: IgE, soluble antigen. Type II: IgG or IgM, cell-bound antigen. Type III: IgG and IgM, soluble antigen. Type IV: T cells. A: Type III. B: Type I. C: Type IV. D: Type IV (CD8).

questions.stem: Which disease is classified as type IV hypersensitivity?
questions.explanation: Type I: anaphylaxis, hay fever. Type II: mismatched transfusion, HDN. Type III: post-streptococcal GN, RA, SLE. Type IV: multiple sclerosis, contact dermatitis, TB test. B: Type III. C: Type I. D: Type II. E: Type III.

questions.stem: Put the steps of a type I reaction in order: (1) mast cell degranulation on re-exposure, (2) activation of Th2 cells and B cells, (3) mast cell sensitization by IgE.
questions.explanation: Step 1: activation of Th2 cell and B cell. Step 2: mast cell sensitization. Step 3: re-exposure to antigen and degranulation. A: Th2 and B-cell activation must produce the IgE first. B: Sensitization precedes degranulation. D: Degranulation is the last step. E: Th2 and B-cell activation comes first.

questions.stem: Which cytokine is crucial for differentiation of Th0 into Th2 cells?
questions.explanation: IL-4 is crucial for the differentiation of Th0 to Th2. A: IL-12 drives Th1 differentiation in the DTH scheme. C: IL-6 drives Th17 differentiation in the DTH scheme. D: IL-5 acts on eosinophils. E: IL-13 promotes mucus production and smooth muscle contraction.

questions.stem: A man stung by a bee collapses within 5 minutes with hypotension and wheezing. Which type of hypersensitivity is this?
questions.explanation: Type I is immediate, within minutes of contact; it includes atopy and anaphylaxis. B: Cell-bound antigen. C: Immune complexes; hours to days. D: Delayed, days. E: Type III, 7–10 days.

questions.stem: A woman with a known peanut allergy reacts within minutes of eating a cookie containing peanut. Why is the reaction so fast?

options.E: IgE is already bound to mast cells

questions.explanation: Sensitization: IgE coats mast cells and basophils; on re-exposure the allergen cross-links IgE and the cells degranulate (histamine, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, tryptase, PAF). A: It is preformed. B: Mast cells do. C: Not the mechanism. D: It is preformed.

questions.stem: What produces the late-phase reaction in type I hypersensitivity?

options.A: Histamine from basophils dilates vessels within minutes
options.B: Immune complexes deposit in vessel walls and fix complement
options.C: Mast-cell chemokines recruit eosinophils and neutrophils
options.D: Th1 cells recruit macrophages through IFN-γ
options.E: IgE is produced de novo by plasma cells at the site

questions.explanation: Mast cells secrete chemokines and other pro-inflammatory mediators, recruiting eosinophils and neutrophils by chemotaxis: the late-phase reaction, with tissue damage and inflammation. A: That is the immediate phase. B: That is type III. D: That is the DTH mechanism. E: Not the mechanism of the late phase.

questions.stem: Which list contains clinical conditions due to type I hypersensitivity?

options.A: Allergic rhinitis, serum sickness and food allergies
options.D: Allergic rhinitis, asthma and food allergies
options.E: Food allergies, Arthus reaction and allergic rhinitis

questions.explanation: Clinical conditions: allergic rhinitis, anaphylaxis, asthma and food allergies. A: Serum sickness is type III. B: Contact dermatitis is type IV. C: Goodpasture syndrome is type II. E: The Arthus reaction is type III.

questions.stem: What is atopy?

options.A: An acquired tendency to produce IgG4 after repeated allergen exposure
options.B: A genetic predisposition to produce IgE to common allergens
options.C: A deficiency of IgE with recurrent parasitic infection
options.D: A delayed T-cell reaction of the skin to contact allergens
options.E: A genetic predisposition to form immune complexes with drugs

questions.explanation: Atopy is the personal tendency (genetic predisposition) to produce IgE antibodies in response to common allergens, with increased risk of asthma, rhinoconjunctivitis or atopic dermatitis. A: Atopy is a genetic tendency to produce IgE. C: Atopy involves IgE production. D: That is contact dermatitis (type IV). E: That is not atopy.

questions.stem: Which antibody class has the lowest plasma level and the shortest half-life (about 2 days)?
questions.explanation: IgE: lowest plasma concentration, shortest half-life (about 2 days), no transplacental transfer. A: About 3 weeks. B: Not the shortest. C: Not the shortest. D: Not the one described.

questions.stem: To which receptor does IgE bind, and on which cells besides mast cells and basophils is it expressed?

options.A: The high-affinity FcεRI; eosinophils and airway smooth muscle
options.B: The low-affinity FcγR; neutrophils, macrophages and NK cells
options.C: The high-affinity FcεRI; red cells, platelets and plasma cells
options.D: Complement receptor CR2; B cells and follicular dendritic cells
options.E: The high-affinity FcεRI; expressed on mast cells and no other cell

questions.explanation: IgE binds the high-affinity FcεRI on basophils, mast cells and eosinophils, and also on airway smooth muscle cells, endothelial cells and epithelial cells. B: That is an IgG receptor. C: Not the cells listed. D: CR2 binds complement fragments. E: It is also on basophils, eosinophils and several tissue cells.

questions.stem: Which mediator is stored preformed in mast cell granules?
questions.explanation: Preformed: histamine and the neutral proteases tryptase and chymase; lipid mediators and Th2 cytokines are also released. A: Lipid mediator, made on activation. B: Lipid mediator, made on activation. D: Lipid mediator, made on activation. E: Not listed as preformed.

questions.stem: Besides IgE cross-linking, which mechanisms can activate mast cells?

options.A: T-cell receptor ligation and CD28 costimulation
options.C: Immune complex deposition and C1 inhibitor binding
options.D: Binding of IgM pentamers to Fc receptors
options.E: Perforin and granzyme release from NK cells

questions.explanation: Mast cells can also be activated through other mechanisms, including complement activation and TLR stimulation. A: Those activate T cells. C: Not the mechanisms named. D: Not named. E: Not named.

questions.stem: An asthmatic patient has marked airway eosinophilia. Which cytokine drives it?
questions.explanation: IL-5: growth, differentiation, activation and survival of eosinophils. IL-13: mucus production and smooth muscle contraction. A: Mucus and smooth muscle contraction. B: Th2 differentiation and IgE. C: Neutrophils. E: Th1, macrophages.

questions.stem: How do the primary and secondary reactions of type I hypersensitivity differ in the lecture figure?

options.A: Primary: begins in 5–30 minutes, lasts about an hour; secondary: begins within 2–7 hours, lasts for days
options.B: Primary: begins within 2–7 hours, lasts for days; secondary: begins in 5–30 minutes, lasts about an hour
options.C: Primary: begins in 5–30 seconds, lasts a minute; secondary: begins in 7–10 days
options.D: Primary: begins in 4–12 hours; secondary: begins in 1–2 days
options.E: Primary: begins in 5–30 minutes, lasts for days; secondary: begins within 2–7 hours, lasts about an hour

questions.explanation: Primary reaction: begins in 5–30 minutes, lasts about an hour (vasodilation, bronchoconstriction, endothelial retraction with leaky vessels and edema). Secondary reaction: begins within 2–7 hours, lasts for days (recruitment of leukocytes; prostaglandins and leukotrienes, the latter excellent bronchoconstrictors). B: Reversed. C: Not the times given. D: These are Arthus and type IV timings. E: Durations are swapped.

questions.stem: Each of the following is listed as a way to test for type I hypersensitivity EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Type I is tested by diagnostic skin testing, immunology laboratory tests, provocation testing and elimination diet. The patch test is used for contact dermatitis (type IV). A: Listed. C: Listed. D: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: When is an immediate skin test read, and which tests are epicutaneous?

options.A: At 15 to 20 minutes; the intradermal test and the patch test
options.B: At 48 to 72 hours; the skin prick test and the scratch test
options.C: At 1 to 2 minutes; the intradermal test
options.D: At 15 to 20 minutes; the skin prick test and the scratch test
options.E: At 4 to 12 hours; the scratch test and the intradermal test

questions.explanation: Small amounts of allergen are introduced into the skin; the wheal and erythema are read at 15 to 20 minutes, when maximal. Epicutaneous tests: skin prick and scratch; the other is the intradermal test. A: The epicutaneous tests are prick and scratch. B: Immediate tests are read at 15–20 minutes. C: Reading is at 15–20 minutes, and the intradermal test is not epicutaneous. E: Not the timing given.

questions.stem: How do the skin prick test and the scratch test differ?

options.A: Prick: a scratch of about 1 cm is made, then allergen is applied; scratch: allergen is applied, then a lancet pricks
options.B: Prick: allergen is injected with a tuberculin syringe; scratch: allergen is applied under a patch
options.C: Prick: read at 15 minutes; scratch: read at 48 hours
options.D: Prick: uses histamine as allergen; scratch: uses saline as allergen
options.E: Prick: allergen is applied, then a lancet pricks the skin; scratch: a scratch of about 1 cm is made, then allergen is applied

questions.explanation: Skin prick test: tiny amounts of allergens are applied and a lancet pricks the surface so extracts can enter. Scratch test: a scratch (about 1 cm) is made and the allergen is then applied. A: Reversed. B: Injection is the intradermal test. C: Both are immediate tests. D: Those are the controls.

questions.stem: A patient took an antihistamine on the morning of skin prick testing. What is expected?

options.A: A wheal at the saline control

questions.explanation: False negatives: prior antihistamines. False positives: bleeding, irritant extracts. Controls: histamine (positive) and saline (negative). A: Not caused by antihistamines. B: The wheal is suppressed. D: Not the effect. E: Causes false positives, not this.

questions.stem: How is the intradermal skin test performed?

options.A: Application of allergen under an occlusive patch on the back for two days
options.B: A lancet prick through a drop of allergen on the forearm
options.C: Inhalation of nebulized allergen with spirometry
options.D: Injection of allergen on the back or arm with a tuberculin syringe
options.E: Injection of histamine into the dermis with a tuberculin syringe

questions.explanation: Intradermal test: small amounts of the allergen are injected intradermally on the back or the arm using a tuberculin syringe; read at 15 to 20 minutes. A: That is patch testing. B: That is the skin prick test. C: That would be a provocation test. E: Histamine is the positive control.

questions.stem: What does an elevated serum tryptase indicate?

options.A: Eosinophil activation, with increased risk of parasitic infection
options.B: Mast cell activation, with increased risk of severe reactions
options.D: T-cell sensitization to a contact allergen

questions.explanation: Tryptase is a marker of mast cell activation; elevated levels indicate an increased risk for severe reactions. A: Tryptase is a mast-cell marker. C: Not what tryptase shows. D: Not what tryptase shows. E: Not the meaning given.

questions.stem: A patient with a previous near-fatal reaction to peanuts needs confirmation of the allergy. Which test is preferable, and why?

options.A: Allergen-specific IgE in blood, given the anaphylaxis risk
options.B: Intradermal skin test, because it is the most sensitive in-vivo test
options.C: Total IgE level, because a normal value rules out allergy
options.D: Patch test, because it detects delayed reactions
options.E: Oral provocation, because history and tests agree

questions.explanation: The assay for allergen-specific IgE antibodies in blood is preferable to in-vivo skin testing when the risk of anaphylaxis is considerable. B: In-vivo testing is avoided when anaphylaxis risk is considerable. C: A normal total IgE does not rule out allergy. D: Patch testing is for contact dermatitis. E: Provocation is used when they disagree, and carries risk.

questions.stem: How should a normal total IgE level be interpreted in a patient with suspected allergy?

options.B: It indicates a type IV mechanism
options.C: It indicates a false-negative skin test
options.D: It predicts a severe reaction on re-exposure
options.E: It does not rule out allergy

questions.explanation: Total IgE is often elevated in allergic patients, but normal IgE levels do not rule out allergy. A: Stated otherwise on the slide. B: Not implied. C: Not implied. D: Tryptase, not total IgE, is tied to severe reactions.

questions.stem: When is a provocation test performed, and how does an elimination diet work?

options.A: When history and confirmatory tests agree; suspected foods are given in increasing doses
options.B: When skin testing is positive; suspected foods are avoided for life
options.C: When history and confirmatory tests disagree; suspected foods are removed, then re-introduced
options.D: When tryptase is elevated; suspected foods are injected intradermally
options.E: When total IgE is normal; suspected foods are applied under a patch

questions.explanation: Provocation tests may be performed when the clinical history and the primary confirmatory tests are discordant. In an elimination diet, suspected food allergens are eliminated then re-introduced and reactions are observed. A: Provocation is for discordant results. B: The diet involves re-introduction. D: Not the method. E: Not the method.

questions.stem: Antibodies binding cell-bound antigens can have three consequences. Which is listed as occurring WITHOUT cell destruction?
questions.explanation: Type II outcomes: (1) cell destruction without inflammation (opsonization and phagocytosis, or antibody-dependent cytotoxicity); (2) complement activation and inflammation; (3) cellular dysfunction without cell destruction. A: This destroys the cell without inflammation. B: This destroys the cell. C: This destroys the cell with inflammation. E: That is type III.

questions.stem: A Rh-negative woman delivers her second Rh-positive baby, who develops hemolytic anemia. What causes it?

options.A: Maternal IgE against fetal red cells
options.C: Maternal T cells crossing the placenta
options.E: Maternal IgG against fetal D antigen

questions.explanation: Rh isoimmunization (type II): the mother is sensitized by the first Rh-positive delivery; her antibodies attack the paternally inherited D antigen on fetal red cells. A: Not type I. B: Not the mechanism. C: Not the mechanism. D: Reversed.

questions.stem: A young man has hemoptysis and rapidly progressive kidney failure from antibodies attacking lung and kidney. What is the antibody target?
questions.explanation: Goodpasture (anti-GBM) syndrome: antibodies attack basement membrane in lungs and kidneys: lung bleeding, glomerulonephritis, kidney failure. A: Graves disease. C: Myasthenia gravis. D: Rh disease. E: SLE.

questions.stem: A woman has hyperthyroidism caused by autoantibodies. What do the antibodies do?

options.B: Kill thyroid cells via CD8 T cells

questions.explanation: Graves: antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor (hyperthyroidism). Myasthenia gravis: antibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptors block transmission. B: Hashimoto disease. C: Myasthenia gravis. D: Not the mechanism. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: A woman with nephritis and arthritis is found to have systemic immune complex disease. Which antibody mainly marks systemic lupus erythematosus?
questions.explanation: Type III: immune complexes deposit in vessels, synovium, glomeruli and alveoli; localized form Arthus, systemic forms serum sickness and SLE (mainly antinuclear antibodies). A: Goodpasture. B: Graves. D: Myasthenia gravis. E: Rh disease.

questions.stem: Which classification of type III reactions is correct?

options.A: Localized: Arthus reaction; systemic: serum sickness and SLE (anti-nuclear antibodies)
options.B: Localized: serum sickness; systemic: Arthus reaction and SLE
options.C: Localized: SLE; systemic: Arthus reaction and contact dermatitis
options.D: Localized: Arthus reaction; systemic: Goodpasture syndrome and Graves disease
options.E: Localized: tuberculin reaction; systemic: serum sickness

questions.explanation: Localized type III: Arthus reaction. Systemic: serum sickness and systemic lupus erythematosus (autoantibodies, mainly anti-nuclear antibodies, deposit in several organs). B: Arthus is local; serum sickness is systemic. C: SLE is systemic and contact dermatitis is type IV. D: Those are type II. E: The tuberculin reaction is type IV.

questions.stem: What is required for an Arthus reaction, and how does it manifest?

options.A: Intradermal antigen in a person not exposed before; local wheal appearing within minutes
options.B: Inhaled antigen in a sensitized person; systemic fever and polyarthritis after a week
options.C: Contact with a hapten on the skin; induration after 1–2 days
options.D: Intravenous foreign serum in large amounts; glomerulonephritis
options.E: Intradermal antigen in a previously sensitized person; local vasculitis of dermal vessels

questions.explanation: The Arthus reaction is in-situ formation of antigen–antibody complexes after intradermal injection of antigen in a previously sensitized person (high antigen and high antibody): local vasculitis from complexes in dermal vessels, with complement activation and recruitment of PMNs. A: Prior sensitization is required, and a wheal within minutes is type I. B: That resembles serum sickness. C: That is type IV. D: That is serum sickness.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old develops severe pain, swelling, induration and hemorrhage at the injection site 8 hours after a tetanus toxoid booster. Which reaction is this?
questions.explanation: Arthus reaction: localized type III, in-situ complexes in a sensitized person; after tetanus or diphtheria toxoid, 4–12 hours after vaccination. A: Minutes, systemic. B: Systemic, 7–10 days. C: Type IV, 1–2 days. E: Infection.

questions.stem: What causes serum sickness?

options.A: Small amounts of intradermal antigen in a sensitized person
options.C: Large amounts of poorly catabolized foreign serum or protein
options.D: Re-exposure to a contact allergen on the skin
options.E: Cross-linking of IgE by a drug hapten

questions.explanation: Serum sickness is a systemic type III reaction due to administration of large amounts of poorly catabolized foreign serum or proteins (antitoxin, antivenom); it first appeared after therapeutic horse antiserum. A: That is the Arthus setting. B: That is SLE. D: That is type IV. E: That is type I.

questions.stem: Ten days after receiving horse antivenom, a patient develops fever, rash and painful joints. Why did symptoms take this long?

options.A: T cells had to be sensitized first
options.B: Antibodies had to be made first

questions.explanation: Serum sickness: systemic type III after foreign serum or protein; symptoms 7–10 days later (time to make antibody); treatment is to withdraw the agent, plus symptomatic drugs. A: Type IV. C: Not the reason. D: Not the reason. E: Not the reason.

questions.stem: How long does the sensitization phase of type IV hypersensitivity take?
questions.explanation: Type IV: sensitization on primary contact (memory T cells, 7–10 days); secondary contact gives tissue damage within 1–2 days. B: Type I. C: Arthus reaction. D: The secondary-contact phase. E: Too long.

questions.stem: Which T cells mediate delayed-type hypersensitivity?
questions.explanation: Type IV subtypes: CD4-mediated delayed-type hypersensitivity; CD8-mediated cytotoxicity. A: Cell-mediated cytotoxicity. B: Not T cells. C: Not the subtype named. D: Not the subtype named.

questions.stem: Two days after weeding, a gardener has an itchy, blistering rash exactly where poison ivy touched her forearms. Which cells drive this reaction?
questions.explanation: Contact dermatitis ("touching") is type IV delayed-type hypersensitivity: urushiol alters self proteins, and CD4+ Th1 cells activate macrophages via IFN-γ, 1–2 days after re-exposure. A: Type I; minutes. C: Type II. D: Type III. E: Type I late phase.

questions.stem: In the Th1 route of delayed-type hypersensitivity, which cytokine activates macrophages?
questions.explanation: Th1 route: IL-12 → Th1 → IFN-γ → macrophages; TNF-α and IL-1β recruit more cells; ROS and lysosomal enzymes damage tissue. Th17 route: IL-6 → Th17 → IL-17 → neutrophils. A: Induces Th1 cells. B: Th17 route, neutrophils. C: Th2. E: Eosinophils.

questions.stem: In the second DTH route shown in the lecture, which cytokines and cells are involved?

options.A: IL-12 induces Th17 cells, whose IL-17 recruits macrophages
options.B: IL-6 induces Th1 cells, whose IFN-γ recruits neutrophils
options.C: IL-6 induces Th17 cells, whose IL-17 recruits neutrophils
options.D: IL-4 induces Th17 cells, whose IL-5 recruits eosinophils
options.E: IL-17 induces Th17 cells, whose IL-6 recruits neutrophils

questions.explanation: Th cells exposed to IL-6 become Th17 cells; IL-17 recruits neutrophils, leading to inflammation and tissue damage. A: IL-6 is the inducer, and neutrophils are recruited. B: IL-6 leads to Th17. D: That mixes in the Th2 pathway. E: The cytokines are swapped.

questions.stem: A nurse develops an itchy vesicular rash on both hands two days after starting to use latex gloves again. Which test confirms the cause?
questions.explanation: Latex contact dermatitis is type IV (DTH); the patch test diagnoses contact dermatitis and finds allergens missed by blood or prick tests. B: Type I. C: Mast cell activation. D: Type I. E: Type I.

questions.stem: Forty-eight hours after an intradermal tuberculin test, a health worker has a 15-mm raised, indurated lesion. Which reaction is this?
questions.explanation: The tuberculin skin test gives a raised, indurated lesion: CD4-mediated delayed-type hypersensitivity (type IV). A: Minutes. C: Hours, hemorrhagic. D: Type II. E: Type III.

questions.stem: Which conditions are given as examples of CD8+ T cell-mediated cytotoxicity?

options.A: Graft rejection after transplant and Graves disease
options.B: Contact dermatitis and the tuberculin reaction
options.D: Graft rejection after transplant and Hashimoto disease

questions.explanation: CD8 cells recognize antigens on cells, causing direct cell destruction. Examples: graft rejection post transplant, Hashimoto disease. A: Graves disease is type II. B: These are DTH (CD4+) examples. C: Myasthenia gravis is type II. E: Serum sickness is type III.

questions.stem: Poison ivy causes contact dermatitis. Which substance is responsible, and to which source of type IV antigens does it belong?

options.A: Urushiol; an autoantigen exposed by tissue injury
options.B: Tuberculin; an antigen from an intracellular pathogen
options.C: Histamine; a preformed mediator in the leaf oil
options.D: Urushiol; a soluble antigen that forms immune complexes
options.E: Urushiol; a foreign chemical that alters self proteins

questions.explanation: Sources of type IV antigens: foreign agents that alter self antigens (urushiol in the surface oil of poison ivy leaves), autoantigens, and antigens from intracellular pathogens causing prolonged infection (mycobacterium). A: It is a foreign chemical altering self proteins. B: Tuberculin relates to mycobacteria. C: Not the mechanism. D: The reaction is T-cell mediated.

questions.stem: Which substance is used as the positive control in skin prick testing?
questions.explanation: Controls: positive histamine (1.8 or 10 mg/mL), negative saline; test sites are spaced apart. A: Negative control. B: Measured in serum. D: Not the control given. E: The test itself.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has drooping eyelids and weakness that worsens through the day. Her antibodies block neuromuscular transmission. What do they target?
questions.explanation: Myasthenia gravis (type II): antibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptors block neuromuscular transmission: weakness and fatigue. A: Graves disease. B: Goodpasture. C: Not the lecture's example. D: Nicotinic.

questions.stem: What is the main treatment of serum sickness?
questions.explanation: Serum sickness: withdraw the agent; anti-inflammatory drugs and antihistamines relieve symptoms. B: Not the treatment given. C: Not the treatment given. D: Type I. E: Not relevant.
